Fit a general logistic model bundle

Source: R/lm-fit.R
fit_logistic.Rd

Fits binary, proportional-odds ordinal, or generalized-logit nominal models under an explicit outcome-level contract. Stacked long-form imputations are fitted separately, one model per imputation. The coefficients are combined with Rubin's rules; the predicted probabilities are averaged per patient.

Usage

fit_logistic(
  formula,
  data,
  family = c("binary", "ordinal", "nominal"),
  outcome_col = NULL,
  id_col = "id",
  imputation_col = NULL,
  outcome_levels,
  event_level = NULL,
  reference_level = NULL,
  prediction_prefix = "prob",
  trace = FALSE
)

Arguments

formula

Model formula.

data

A data frame containing the outcome and predictors.

family

Model family: "binary" (default, stats::glm() with a logit link), "ordinal" (proportional-odds cumulative logit, MASS::polr(); a two-level outcome is fitted with stats::glm()) or "nominal" (generalized logit, nnet::multinom()).

outcome_col

Outcome column. By default it is read from formula.

id_col

Patient identifier column. Default "id". Required, and checked, only when imputation_col is set, where it aligns each patient's rows across imputations.

imputation_col

Imputation-index column, or NULL for one dataset.

outcome_levels

Complete outcome levels in their declared order.

event_level

Event level for a binary model.

reference_level

Reference level for a nominal model.

prediction_prefix

Name for a binary probability column, or prefix for ordinal and nominal level-specific probability columns.

trace

Whether model engines should print fitting progress.

Value

An object of class c("lm_fit", "ps_data") with:

$data

data (the lowest-numbered imputation when imputation_col is set, without that column) with the predicted probabilities appended: one column named prediction_prefix for a binary model (prob by default), the probability of event_level; or one <prediction_prefix>_<level> column per outcome level for an ordinal or nominal model, whose outcome column is returned as a factor (ordered for an ordinal model). A row missing a predictor has missing probabilities.

$meta

Named list: bundle_version (1), formula, outcome_col, model_family, outcome_levels, event_level (binary only, else NULL), reference_level (nominal only, else NULL), cumulative_direction (ordinal only, else NULL), predictors, id_col, imputation_col, n_imputations, n_input, n_analyzed, n_excluded (summed over imputations), prediction_prefix and package_versions (R, this package and the model engine).

$tables

Named list: estimates (one row per term: term, estimate, std.error, statistic, df, p.value, conf.low, conf.high, odds_ratio (NA for an ordinal threshold), and pooled, TRUE when Rubin's rules combined imputations; a pooled df is Barnard and Rubin's, see "Pooled degrees of freedom"), covariance (the coefficient covariance matrix, pooled when imputed), by_imputation (imputation, term, estimate, std.error) and fit_status (one row per imputation: imputation, converged, n_input, n_analyzed, n_excluded).

$models

The fitted models, one per imputation, named by imputation index ("1" for a single dataset). For binary bundles, validate_logistic() scores new data with them; it rejects ordinal and nominal bundles.

Details

Multiple imputation. With imputation_col set, one model is fitted to each imputed dataset. The two outputs are then combined differently. $tables$estimates and $tables$covariance pool the coefficients and their variances with Rubin's rules, with Barnard and Rubin's degrees of freedom (see "Pooled degrees of freedom" below). The probability columns in $data are the per-patient mean, on the probability scale, of the predictions from each imputation's model. Rubin's rules play no part there: averaging the predictions is what Leyrat et al. (2019) call the "across" approach. For a propensity score they favour the "within" approach instead; see ps_logistic() for the recipe.

$data is built from the lowest-numbered imputation: its rows, ordered as they appear there, its covariate values, and no imputation_col.

Pooled degrees of freedom

With imputation_col set, each pooled coefficient is tested against a t distribution, and the df column of $tables$estimates gives its degrees of freedom. We use Barnard and Rubin's (1999) small-sample degrees of freedom, computed the way mice::pool() computes them, so a pooled table here and one from mice agree.

Rubin's (1987) original degrees of freedom are \(\nu_{old} = (m - 1) / \lambda^2\), where \(m\) is the number of imputations and \(\lambda = (1 + 1/m) B / T\) is the proportion of a coefficient's total variance \(T\) due to missing data, through the between-imputation variance \(B\). (This is lambda in mice, not its finite-sample fraction of missing information, fmi.) When little is missing, \(\lambda\) is small and \(\nu_{old}\) can run into the millions, larger than the sample could ever support, and the intervals come out too narrow. Barnard and Rubin cap it with the complete-data degrees of freedom \(\nu_{com}\), the value the analysis would have had with no missing data: $$\nu_{obs} = \frac{\nu_{com} + 1}{\nu_{com} + 3} \nu_{com} (1 - \lambda), \qquad \nu = \left(\frac{1}{\nu_{old}} + \frac{1}{\nu_{obs}}\right)^{-1}.$$ So \(\nu\) never exceeds \(\nu_{com}\), and it approaches \(\nu_{old}\) as \(\nu_{com}\) grows.

\(\nu_{com}\) is \(n - k\), the residual degrees of freedom of the first imputation's model: \(n\) analysed patients minus \(k\) estimated parameters. That holds for every family, linear, logistic, ordinal, nominal and count, as it does in mice. nnet::multinom() reports no residual degrees of freedom, so for a nominal model \(k\) is its effective degrees of freedom, again as mice does. Pooling stops with an error when \(\nu_{com}\) is zero or negative, as it is for a saturated model, because no small-sample degrees of freedom exist then.

Two consequences are worth knowing. First, a single logistic, ordinal, nominal or count fit is tested against the normal distribution (df is Inf), but the same model pooled over imputations reports a finite df and a t test. A single linear fit uses its residual degrees of freedom. Second, SAS PROC MIANALYZE reports \(\nu_{old}\) unless you give it the complete-data degrees of freedom with EDF=. To reproduce these df, and the p-values and intervals that depend on them, run PROC MIANALYZE with EDF= set to \(n - k\).

Barnard J, Rubin DB (1999). Small-sample degrees of freedom with multiple imputation. Biometrika, 86(4), 948–955. doi:10.1093/biomet/86.4.948

Rubin DB (1987). Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys. Wiley. doi:10.1002/9780470316696

References

Leyrat C, Seaman SR, White IR, Douglas I, Smeeth L, Kim J, Resche-Rigon M, Carpenter JR, Williamson EJ (2019). Propensity score analysis with partially observed covariates: how should multiple imputation be used? Statistical Methods in Medical Research, 28(1), 3–19. doi:10.1177/0962280217713032

Examples

dta <- sample_ps_data(n = 150, seed = 42)
fit <- fit_logistic(
  tavr ~ age + female + ef,
  data           = dta,
  family         = "binary",
  outcome_levels = c(0, 1),
  event_level    = 1
)
fit$tables$estimates[, c("term", "estimate", "odds_ratio")]
#>          term    estimate odds_ratio
#> 1 (Intercept)  3.55713646 35.0626500
#> 2         age -0.09113276  0.9128965
#> 3      female  0.18166589  1.1992135
#> 4          ef  0.05839068  1.0601291
head(fit$data[, c("id", "tavr", "prob")])
#>   id tavr      prob
#> 1  1    0 0.1657534
#> 2  2    0 0.5493138
#> 3  3    0 0.2856728
#> 4  4    0 0.2041096
#> 5  5    0 0.5254897
#> 6  6    0 0.3978214
